newsitem.title: SPAIN: Bank of Spain says inflation goals easily met.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Spain says inflation goals easily met.

text.p: Spain's economy has abundantly out-performed even the most optimistic forecasts, making it likely to match inflation levels of the most stable European economies, Bank of Spain research director Jose Luis Malo de Molina said in a prepared speech on Monday.
"The deflation (falling inflation) has been much more rapid and energetic than hoped, even in the most optimistic scenarios," he said at the Royal Academy for Political Science.

"The prospects are very favourable not only for meeting the convergence criteria in this area but for also achieving successive objectives to consolidate inflation levels near those in the most stable countries of the EU."

Malo de Molina said it was ironic that just as an active Bank of Spain monetary policy had started yield results, as seen in the economic stability, is when it was to give up its sovereignty to the European Monetary Union (EMU).

He said Spain's participation from the start of EMU would be: "The happy culmination of a long and arduous battle to put an active monetary policy capable of generating macroeconomic stabiliy in place."
But Malo de Molina added, it would happen "exactly as its autonomous monetary policy was diluted in the new united monetary policy of the EMU."

The central bank director said the process of reducing inflation, which was 1.7 percent in April after 2.2 percent in March, was "very fortunate" for the framework fixed by the Bank of Spain in 1994 when it was given the role of guaranteeing consumer price stability.

"The success in this first phase of application is not limited only to the comfortable compliance and the early reaching of set goals, but also in the way the different related variables had reacted," he said.

The rise in intervention rates to combat inflation at the start of 1995 had resulted -- after an initial period of nervousness -- in a progressive strengthening of the exchange rate, an increase in long-term rates and a skewed yield curve.

Eventually, market confidence in the gradually improving prospectives with a reduction in inflation materialising had paved the way for lower rates and a the return of a normal yield curve that was at a "considerable lower level more in line with core EU countries."
